readerTitle: Your plan works until your rival answers
caseNote: 가상 사례 (라멘 가게 두 곳, 프로젝트 관리 앱) + 실제 연구 (von Neumann & Morgenstern 1944, Dixit & Nalebuff 1991) · 모든 수치는 설명용. 확인된 실제 기업 사례가 마땅치 않아 company_story 대신 everyday_scene으로 바꿈
insight: 내 결정의 결과는 상대의 대응까지 합쳐서 정해진다. 결정하기 전에 상대 자리에 앉아 '그들은 어떻게 답할까'를 먼저 계산한다.
misconception: 좋은 계획은 시장 크기와 내 비용만 계산하면 된다. 경쟁자는 내가 움직여도 그대로 있을 것이다.

sources.text: von Neumann, J. & Morgenstern, O. (1944). Theory of Games and Economic Behavior. Princeton University Press.
Dixit, A. & Nalebuff, B. (1991). Thinking Strategically. W. W. Norton. ('Look forward, reason back')
라멘 가게와 앱 사례의 모든 수치는 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: 라멘 가게 계산: 혼자 심야 영업 시 월 매출 $6,000 − 야간 인건비 등 $4,000 = +$2,000. 둘 다 영업 시 매출을 나눠 $3,000 − $4,000 = 각각 −$1,000. 아무도 안 하면 $0. 상대만 하면 나는 $0으로 단순화(단골 일부 이탈은 무시).
'Look forward, reason back'은 Dixit & Nalebuff(1991) Thinking Strategically의 표현으로 알려져 있음. 게시 전 원문 문구 확인 필요.
von Neumann & Morgenstern의 책이 1944년 출간되어 게임이론을 하나의 분야로 세웠다는 서술은 일반적인 학계 설명. 게시 전 재확인.

cards.title: Your plan works until your rival answers
body: Two ramen shops share one busy street. One owner decides to stay open until 1 a.m. to catch the after-work crowd.
For two weeks, it's a hit. Then the shop across the street starts staying open late too. Now both pay night staff, and they split the same tired customers.
The plan wasn't wrong. It just assumed nobody would answer.

image.label: Two ramen shops facing each other on a night street, both lit up
image.brief: 밤거리, 길을 사이에 두고 마주 보는 라멘 가게 두 곳. 왼쪽 가게는 불이 켜져 있고, 오른쪽 가게도 막 간판 불을 켜는 순간. 손님은 몇 명뿐. 실제 상호나 로고는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: Should you stay open late?
body: You run one of the shops. Your estimate: late-night customers would bring in $6,000 a month. Night staff and costs run $4,000. That's $2,000 extra profit.
Your rival can copy late hours with one week of hiring. What do you do?

options.text: Go ahead. The numbers show +$2,000 a month
options.feedback: The math is right for a street with one shop. It ignores the one person most likely to change it.

options.text: First work out what your rival would do in response, and what you'd earn then
options.feedback: You give up a quick start, but you see the real result before you pay for it. The next card shows why it matters.

options.text: Move fast. Whoever opens late first keeps the crowd
options.feedback: Speed can build habits. But if copying takes one week, being first buys you very little time.

cards.title: Your result depends on two choices, not one.
body: If your rival follows, you each earn $3,000 but still pay $4,000. Your **+$2,000** becomes **−$1,000**.

breakdown.label: Only the rival opens late
breakdown.detail: Simplified: you keep your day trade

cards.title: Game theory
body: **Game theory** is the study of choices where your result depends on what others choose, and theirs depends on yours.
Every game has three parts: the *players* who decide, the *moves* each can make, and the *payoffs* each gets from every combination of moves.
A normal decision is you against the weather. A game is you against someone who thinks back.

image.label: A two-by-two grid of outcomes with a player on each side
image.brief: 2×2 표 인포그래픽. 왼쪽에 'You: open late / stay closed', 위쪽에 'Rival: open late / stay closed'. 각 칸에 위 카드의 금액. 'Both open late' 칸(−$1,000)을 강조 색으로.

cards.title: Look forward, reason back.
body: Mathematician John von Neumann and economist Oskar Morgenstern turned this way of thinking into a field in their 1944 book. Later, economists Avinash Dixit and Barry Nalebuff summed up the habit in four words: *look forward, reason back*.
list: **Look forward:** list your move, then each answer the other side could give
**Score it:** what does each player earn in each case?
**Reason back:** assume they pick what's best for them, then choose your move
cards.callout: For the ramen shop, reasoning back shows late hours lose money unless something stops the rival from copying.

cards.title: Rivals aren't the only players.
body: Suppliers, staff, landlords and customers all answer your moves. Raise a supplier's order size, and they may change their prices. Change a bonus rule, and staff change what they work on.

Some choices aren't games at all. A farmer selling wheat into a huge market can plan alone, because no single buyer or rival notices. Game thinking matters most when **a few players watch each other** closely.

cards.title: The map is never the real street.
body: Real people don't always choose what's best for them. Your rival may not notice you, may be too busy, or may react out of pride. Treat your prediction as a guess and watch what actually happens.

And not every game is win-lose. If both shops stay open late, the street may become known for late-night food and draw new customers. Check whether the total can grow before you assume you must split it.

cards.title: Now it's a software app.
body: You run a project-management app for small agencies. A similar-sized rival charges for exporting reports, and so do you. You're thinking of making export free to win their users.
Their team could copy the change in a week. What's your move?

options.text: Make export free and announce it loudly
options.feedback: You may win users for a week or two. If the rival matches, you both lose export revenue and the users stay put.

options.text: Skip it, and invest in something hard to copy, like integrations agencies rely on
options.feedback: It's slower and costs more to build. But a move the rival can't answer quickly keeps paying off after they react.

options.text: Make export free only for new sign-ups this month
options.feedback: It limits the revenue you lose. But the rival can still match it, and you've trained buyers to wait for deals.

cards.title: Before you move, ask how they'll answer.
body: Your move plus their answer decides your result. A plan that only works if nobody reacts is a bet, not a plan.
**Try it today:** pick one change you're planning. Write down who could respond, their two most likely answers, and what you'd earn in each case.
